Figure caption: Illustrated the preparation and action mechanisms of LNP-siRNA/GM nanoparticles. LNP-siRNA/GM nanoparticles were prepared using microfluidic chip technology based on interaction among lipid materials, siRNA, and GM. After cellular internalization, LNP-siEGFR/GM exerted the antitumor effect following a multi-pathway . First, GM enhanced EGFR-siRNA endo‐lysosomal escape and improved the delivery efficiency. Second, the expansion of EGFR silencing by GM inhibited the tumor cells growth. Third, GM downregulated VEGF and CXCL12 synergistically inhibiting tumors.

Figure caption: Free GM was identified as siRNA delivery-promoting of LNPs. (A) Cytotoxicity of free GM with different concentrations in A549-Luc cells (n = 6). (B) Normalized bioluminescence intensity after pretreatment with various free GM of LNP-siRNA transfection (n = 4). (C) CLSM imaging of colocalization (yellow) of Cy5-siRNA nanoparticles (red) and endo‐lysosomes (green) and (D) quantitative analysis of co-localization in A549-Luc cells pretreatment with free GM of LNP-siRNA transfection (n = 5). The data are shown as mean ± SD. *P < 0.05, ⁎⁎P < 0.01, and ⁎⁎⁎P < 0.001.

Figure caption: Characterization of LNP-siRNA/GM and LNP-siRNA. (A) Size and zeta potential of LNP-siRNA/GM and LNP-siRNA. (B) SEM image of LNP-siRNA/GM (scale bar: 200 nm). (C) EE of GM LNP-siRNA/GM. (D) EE of siRNA of LNP-siRNA/GM and LNP-siRNA. (E) Protective effects of LNP-siRNA/GM on preventing siRNA aggregation induced by serum proteins. (F) Dilution stability and (G) storage stability of LNP-siRNA/GM. The data are shown as mean ± SD (n = 3).

Figure caption: In vitro siRNA internalization and transfection efficiency of LNP-siRNA/GM. (A) CLSM imaging of cell uptake incubated with Cy5-siRNA nanoparticles (red), rhodamine phalloidin (green) for cell skeleton and Hoechst 33342 (blue) for nucleus, scale bars: 50 µm. (B) Intracellular fluorescence intensity detected by flow cytometry with the FAM-siRNA nanoparticles (n = 4). (C) Intracellular fluorescence intensity detected by flow cytometry after nanoparticles treatments with different inhibitors (n = 4). (D) Normalized bioluminescence intensity after LNP-siRNA/GM treatments with various GM concentration (n = 5). (E) Normalized bioluminescence intensity after nanoparticles treatments with various siRNA concentration (n = 6). The data are shown as mean ± SD.*P < 0.05, ⁎⁎P < 0.01, and ⁎⁎⁎P < 0.001.

Figure caption: Enhancement of siRNA endo‐lysosomal escape and its mechanism by GM. (A-B) CLSM imaging of colocalization (yellow) of Cy5-siRNA nanoparticles (red) and endo‐lysosomes (green) in A549-Luc cells and HepG2 cells, scale bars: 20 µm. (C-D) Quantitative analysis of co-localization in A549-Luc cells and HepG2 cells (n = 5). (E) LDR signal change measured by cytometry after nanoparticles treatments (n = 4). (F) CLSM images for the phospholipid distribution visualized after treatment with different nanoparticles. The phospholipid was stained with LipidTOX™ (yellow), scale bar: 50 µm. (G) CLSM images for the ROS distribution visualized after treatment with different nanoparticles. The ROS was stained with DCFH-DA (green), scale bar: 50 µm. (H) CLSM images of AO staining for the endo‐lysosomal disruption test with different nanoparticles, scale bar: 100 µm. (I) CLSM images showing galectin-3 (yellow) endo‐lysosomal disruption visualized after treatment with different nanoparticles. The nucleus was stained with Hoechst 33342 (blue) for all images, scale bar: 20 µm. The data are shown as mean ± SD. *P < 0.05, ⁎⁎P < 0.01, and ⁎⁎⁎P < 0.001.

Figure caption: In vitro biological activities of nanoparticles. (A) HepG2 Inhibition effects after incubation with 25 mM, 100 mM, 200 mM siRNA nanoparticles (n = 6). (B-C) Relative expression levels of EGFR mRNA (n = 4) and EGFR protein (n = 3) detected by RT-PCR and ELISA Kit. (D-E) HepG2 cells apoptosis images and quantitative analysis of apoptosis rate (n = 4). (F) Live-dead cell staining on HepG2 in vitro after treatment with different nanoparticles, scale bar: 100 µm. (G) Tube formation effect on HUVECs in vitro after treatment with different nanoparticles and (H) quantitative analysis of mesh index, scale bar: 200 µm. (n = 3). (I-J) Relative expression levels of VEGF and CXCL12 protein detected by ELISA Kit (n = 3). The data are shown as mean ± SD. *P < 0.05, ⁎⁎P < 0.01 and ⁎⁎⁎P < 0.001.

Figure caption: The biodistribution of nanoparticles in Balb/c tumor-bearing nude mice. (A-B) Imaging of resected organs and tumor from mice after administrated intravenous injection Cy5-siRNA nanoparticles for 12 h and 36 h. (n = 4) [Radiant Efficiency × 108: (p/s/cm2/sr)/(µW/cm2)]. (C-D) Quantitative analysis of average radiant efficiency (n = 4). The data are shown as mean ± SD. *P < 0.05, ⁎⁎P < 0.01 and ⁎⁎⁎P < 0.001.

Figure caption: In vivo anti-tumor effects of nanoparticles in Balb/c tumor-bearing nude mice. (A) Schematic treatment schedule in vivo. (B) Tumor growth curves after treatment with nanoparticles in mice (n = 6). (C) Tumor weight at the end of treatment in mice (n = 6). (D) The relative EGFR mRNA levels in tumor tissue detected by RT-PCR (n = 4). (E) Images of H&E staining after treatment with nanoparticles in mice (n = 6), scale bar: 300 µm. The data are shown as mean ± SD. Statistical significance was calculated by t-tests comparison between two groups. *P < 0.05, ⁎⁎P < 0.01, and ⁎⁎⁎P < 0.001.

Figure caption: In vivo tumor histological pathology examination and VEGF and CXCL12 protein levels. (A) EGFR immunohistochemistry stained images of tumor tissues, scale bar: 300 µm, enlarged view (scale bar: 60 µm). (B)Quantitative analysis of percentage area stained(n = 6). (C-D) Relative expression levels of VEGF and CXCL12 protein detected by ELISA Kit (n = 6) (E-G) CD31, Ki67 and TUNEL immunofluorescence stained images of tumor tissues, scale bar: 100 µm. *P < 0.05, ⁎⁎P < 0.01 and ⁎⁎⁎P < 0.001.
